title: Personal Research Ontologies for Personal Open Science | Proceedings of the 14th ACM Collective Intelligence Conference
content: Abstract: As researchers conduct their work, they incrementally construct a personal research ontology: a rich, personal understanding of their field and its phenomena. Yet most of this knowledge remains internalized, with only fragments surfacing in publications. This position paper argues that research is fundamentally an act of personal ontology construction and proposes Personal Open Science (POS), a lightweight method for externalizing a researcher’s personal research ontology for downstream use. The method requires no machine learning or language models, and it centers on the researcher rather than on the publication, the traditional focal unit of Open Science. Building on daily reading habits and a minimal annotation scheme, the approach adds little overhead while producing a structured, explorable representation of a researcher’s interests, influences, and expertise. I demonstrate the method through my own practice of annotating over 45,000 documents across a decade of research. title: Open Access in the European Research Area: progress remains uneven as new report calls for more concerted action - Research and innovation
content:
"A new independent expert report published today by the European Commission highlights that, despite notable advancement, the implementation of open access across the European Research Area remains uneven and fragmented. While progress has been made, persistent barriers continue to hinder widespread open access, and further action is needed.

Over the past decade, European Union soft-law measures, national strategies, funder mandates, and, where applicable, national legislation have advanced open access. However, these efforts have not yet produced a coherent framework across the European Research Area, leaving researchers, institutions, and funders to navigate differing policies.

The report provides a snapshot of the current open access landscape, offering policy recommendations to improve access to scientific publications and research data. It draws on an analysis of all 27 EU Member States and eight non-EU countries."

title: Reframing Repositories – COAR
content:
"Scholarly communication is at a crossroads. Scholarly infrastructure has become dangerously concentrated in the hands of a small number of commercial publishers and foreign-controlled platforms, leaving institutions and nations exposed to disruptions they cannot control.

At the same time, the integrity of the scientific record is under acute strain, as AI-generated fabrications, paper mills, and reproducibility failures erode the trust on which science depends and public trust in information is fragile, at precisely the moment when citizens most need reliable access to evidence. Repositories help to address all of these challenges.

To highlight the critical importance of repositories, COAR is publishing a “Narrative Series”. The series provides several compelling, evidence-based portrayals that, taken together, build a powerful case for repositories as essential infrastructure for scholarly communications and the global knowledge commons."

These blog posts are a series of ‘explainer’ pre-reading to start participants thinking about the issues the course considered in relation to the general decline of scholarly publishing. The blog posts in this series considered the problem of questionable research practices, the mechanisms to manage these through corrections and retractions, the problem of university rankings and the uneasy nexus between Open and AI. They finish with some suggestions of where we go from here."

title: Can open science speak qualitative? Rearticulating open science vocabulary for qualitative research
content: Abstract: ‘Open research’ (or ‘open science’) has substantially reshaped conversations surrounding rigor, transparency, and accountability, yet its vocabulary remains largely rooted in quantitative, positivist paradigms. Terms such as reproducibility, replicability, and generalisability are routinely treated as universal markers of research quality, despite their limited epistemological compatibility with many qualitative methodologies. While qualitative scholars have long articulated the limitations this, the rapid emergence of the open research movement creates a new context to synthesise and translate these ideas. Drawing on established traditions and debates, we propose a rearticulation of open research terminology that better reflects interpretive logics and methodological pluralism of many qualitative approaches. Specifically, we advocate for concepts such as ‘traceability’ to replace ‘reproducibility’, ‘transferability’ rather than ‘generalisability’, and ‘dependability’ instead of ‘replicability’. title: Open science interventions to improve reproducibility in science: a narrative review from a behaviour change wheel perspective | Royal Society Open Science | The Royal Society
content: Abstract: Academics, policymakers and other research stakeholders have broadly discussed strategies to improve research reproducibility, with heightened attention given to open science practices. One strand of these discussions adopts a behavioural perspective centred on researchers. This narrative review applied the behaviour change wheel (BCW) framework to analyse 103 interventions evaluated for their effectiveness in improving reproducibility and reproducibility-related practices. We systematically mapped the included interventions across the nine BCW intervention types and seven supporting policy categories, highlighting which mechanisms have been most and least frequently evaluated empirically. We then interpreted these mechanisms using the COM-B behaviour model (capability–opportunity–motivation). The analysis revealed that ‘coercion’ and ‘persuasion’ were the most commonly studied types of intervention, implemented through ‘regulations’ and ‘guidelines’, with active enforcement appearing to be more effective than voluntary adherence. title: Utrecht University Open Access Policy 2026-2030 | Zenodo
content: Abstract:  The Utrecht University Open Access Policy 2026-2030 sets out goals and actions to improve open access of publications by authors affiliated to Utrecht University and the UMC Utrecht. It does so building on a set of values and aligning with national and international frameworks for open access and open science in general. The policy both widens and deepens the scope compared to the previous policy: more publication types beyond articles and books are in scope and more aspects of open access publishing are being addressed. In particular, the policy adresses knowledge equity and governance and digital autonomy, next to openness, copyright retention and licensing, timing and metadata. The policy works in tandem with Utrecht University's recognition and rewards policy and procedures, and with any faculty and departmental publishing strategies.

title: New open access policy determined - News - Utrecht University
content:
"The Utrecht University Executive Board has determined the new open access policy. The policy came into effect this year and is valid until the end of 2030. It is being coordinated by Utrecht University Library.

What is new?

Open access now no longer only concerns journal articles and books, but all publications that report on research. For instance: conference proceedings, reports, preprints and professional publications. The policy supports making all these kinds of publications open access available. That way it becomes easier to select the publication type which best reaches the target group.

The new policy also aims to improve the digital autonomy and knowledge equity in publishing. We stimulate ways of publishing where the research community is at the helm, rather than the big, commercial publishers. In this way we support publication routes without fees being charged to readers as well as the authors (diamond open access) and routes that are based on preprints (publish-review-curate)."

content: "Since 2018, the year the First French Plan for Open Science was adopted, France has played a leading role in developing open science. There are numerous indicators that demonstrate this, thanks in particular to the French Open Science Monitor, which provides an overview of publications, PhDs, data, software, clinical trials, and institutional policies. The French open science policy enjoys broad support from higher education and research institutions (it is considered useful by 95% of them). As primary stakeholders, they are closely involved in the governance of open science through the French Committee for Open Science and the French Open Science Fund, and are able to implement local versions of the French Open Science Monitor. Institutions have also responded actively to initiatives aimed at consolidating or launching major open science infrastructures for making publications accessible (HAL), sharing data (creation of Recherche Data Gouv), and preserving the world's software assets (Software Heritage).... title: Large Scale Digitization in the AI Era | Center for Research Libraries
content:
"Libraries are increasingly being approached about partnerships that would digitize collections at scale and potentially make the resulting digital content and metadata available for commercial artificial intelligence or other proprietary services. These proposals may offer significant benefits—including expanded access, preservation, and reduced digitization costs—but they also raise questions about ownership, permitted uses, public access, institutional control, compensation, attribution, privacy, and long-term stewardship.

CRL member library directors have identified a need for clearer guidance about the terms libraries should seek when considering these arrangements. Decisions made by individual institutions may also shape emerging practices across the library community and affect how collectively stewarded scholarly and cultural resources are used."

This study is the first of its type to present a comprehensive overview of the project’s objectives methodologies and results. The aim is to assess the impact of the transition form traditional archiving practices to digital applications. This is particularly important in the field of theses and dissertations. Based on project documents reports from participating institutions and observations on the archiving processes software used, digitization techniques, and data management processes, a qualitative case study approach was employed. The project resulted in easier access to academic content reduced the administrative workload, and reduced the risk of data loss and damage. content: Abstract: Scholarly communication platforms have become essential tools for enhancing research visibility, collaboration, and knowledge dissemination in higher education institutions. Despite these benefits, their effective utilization remains constrained by several organizational, technological, and human-related factors, particularly within military institutions where information management is influenced by security protocols and hierarchical administrative structures. This study investigated the challenges affecting the utilization of scholarly communication platforms for information sharing among librarians in military institutions in Northern Nigeria and assessed the impact of these challenges on platform utilization. A quantitative survey research design was adopted, involving a census of 130 librarians from the Nigerian Defence Academy Kaduna, the Nigerian Army University Biu, and the Air Force Institute of Technology Kaduna. title: Leveraging knowledge management to enhance research access and visibility via institutional repositories in South African universities
content: Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine how South African universities are applying knowledge management practices to enhance the effectiveness of institutional repositories in improving research access and visibility. Design/methodology/approach – The research was conducted using a qualitative content analysis, gathering data from secondary sources and organising it according to the stages of knowledge management: knowledge capture, organisation and storage, dissemination and application. Findings – All universities in South Africa have implemented repositories, yet their alignment with knowledge management outcomes is lacking. Poor alignment between repository goals and knowledge management outcomes, limited institutional support, fragmentation and siloed practices contributed to the underutilisation of repository systems. title: To sign or not to sign initiatives to reform research evaluation: A discussion of the pros and cons - ScienceDirect
content: Abstract: The integration of bibliometrics into science governance has fundamentally transformed scientific practices, leading to unintended consequences such as goal displacement and citizen bibliometrics. In response, international reform movements like the Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment (CoARA) advocate for responsible research assessment and the primacy of qualitative peer review. This short communication examines the commonalities and differences of these movements and weighs the pros and cons for research organizations considering signing them. While endorsement offers socio-political legitimacy and can catalyze internal modernization toward improved evaluation processes, organizations are also confronted with certain challenges. These include the potential neglect of disciplinary evaluation cultures, the high administrative burden of qualitative review, and the prevalent risk of purely symbolic uptake. Acknowledging the limitations of current empirical evidence, this commentary concludes that the future of research assessment relies not on universal declarations, but on the development of process-specific evaluation designs. title: Awareness of Predatory Journals and Open Access: an online survey among Italian Researchers | JLIS.it
content: Abstract: This study investigates Italian academics’ awareness, perceptions, and experiences of predatory publishing, a phenomenon recognised as a threat to research integrity and scholarly communication. An online survey of researchers affiliated with Italian universities and research institutes yielded 258 responses, which were analysed. Results show that awareness of predatory publishing is high: almost half of respondents (47.9%) had discussed it with colleagues, and more than one-third had encountered it as authors, reviewers, or readers. Familiarity varies across dimensions, with predatory journals and spam emails being most recognised, and fraudulent websites and podcasts less so. 30% of participants reported personal experience of editorial misleading, mainly as authors, and 76% had received spam or phishing solicitations. Significant differences emerged by professional title and age, with senior researchers demonstrating greater awareness and greater exposure to training. Most participants perceive predatory publishing as having a moderate or high impact on scientific integrity, but only half have received training in research ethics or use verification tools. title: Public Knowledge: Why "Open" Matters with Christopher Marcum
content:
"In the Season 3 premiere of Educating to Be Human, we launch a series-long exploration of “open”, in conversations with people who are working to ensure that public data, knowledge, and research remain open and freely accessible for all. Host Lisa Petrides is joined by sociologist and open science advocate Christopher Marcum, former Assistant Director for Open Science and Data Policy at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP).

In this conversation, Lisa and Chris trace the origins of open from its 17th-century roots and Robert Merton’s 1940s ideal of knowledge as a non-excludable public good to the modern policies governing taxpayer-funded research today. Together, they confront the mounting threats facing open systems - from big tech monopolies and AI data scraping to the rise of closed digital gatekeepers - and explore why open infrastructure is as vital to a thriving society as physical roads and bridges. This episode challenges us to rethink how we protect public knowledge, sustain open infrastructure, and cultivate the human curiosity necessary to question the technological systems shaping our world."

title: OpenAIRE and the Next Phase of Open Research Information in the Netherlands
content:
"This year has marked an important moment for Open Research Information in the Netherlands. A new wave of initiatives is turning long-standing ambitions around openness, interoperability, and digital sovereignty into concrete implementation. Projects such as DURF, BROCCOLI, MORIS, and the ongoing PID-to-Portal work are not isolated experiments. Together, they point to a broader national effort to make Dutch research information more visible, reusable, and trustworthy across institutions and systems. 

In this transition, OpenAIRE has a meaningful role to play. As a European, community-governed organisation, it brings experience in building and sustaining open scholarly communication services. Through the OpenAIRE Graph and related services, it also supports the infrastructure layer needed to connect, enrich, and expose research information across institutional and national contexts."

title: Open Data in the Arts | Open Research Bulletin
content: Abstract:  At its inception, Open Access (OA) was created as a new way of freely sharing traditional research outputs such as peer-reviewed journal content to all ‘scientists, scholars, teachers, students, and other curious minds’ via the internet (Budapest Open Access Initiative, 2002). Since then, OA has become a cornerstone of a wide variety of research practices across many discipline areas, enabling academics to instantly access current research, and allowing the public to access taxpayer-funded innovations (UKRN, 2020; UKRN 2024a). This success has led to an expansion of the concept of ‘openness’ in research, making space for further paradigms such as Open Data whereby ‘evidence that underpins the answer to the research question, and can be used to validate findings’ are made open under licenses which permit reuse (UKRI, 2016:3). Open Data is rapidly becoming an important part of research, as more journals require data access statements to be provided as part of published papers due to an increased number of funders requiring research data to be made ‘as open as possible, as closed as necessary’ (H2020 Programme, 2016).

title: A Reasonable Request for Data and Coding Transparency | Open Research Bulletin
content: Abstract:  Not long ago, I had disparate experiences engaging with two different publications. The first was from a research group I knew and liked. Their article included results that were aligned with what I already knew, but I had a few queries about the analysis. As the data were ‘available on reasonable request’, I promptly made such a request. Although the first author wrote to explain some of the findings to me, they did not share their data and I could not confirm the results. In contrast, the second article was published by a group that I had known to be under scrutiny, and I admit that initially I was critical of the results. However, as their data and analysis scripts were published and accessible (in this case, on the Open Science Framework), I was able to not only confirm the results but also conclude that they had reported them conservatively. In these cases, data (un-)availability influenced my confidence in the research. The inconsistent experiences I have had with data availability emphasise the importance of improving the openness of data in research.

title: Data Management Planning for Open and Reproducible Research | Open Research Bulletin
content: Abstract:  The term Data Management Plan (DMP) can elicit reluctance, scepticism and sometimes even an eye roll from overworked and overstretched researchers, who can view it as an unwelcome administrative burden. In reality, a well-considered DMP is an incredibly valuable project document that underpins open and reproducible research, supporting future reuse by both the research team and others. As the volume and complexity of research data continue to increase, researchers benefit from clear, practical approaches to data storage, security and sharing. This article outlines the core elements of an effective DMP, pitfalls to avoid and how DMPs enable Open Research through responsible data sharing and long-term preservation. It also highlights tools and support available to help researchers create DMPs that are useful throughout the project and beyond.

title: Ribaric | Constructing a (Meaningful) Scholarly Publishing Narrative: Bootstrapping Green Open Access Submissions for Open Access Week | Journal of Librarianship and Scholarly Communication
content: Abstract: Introduction: Green Open Access requires authors to submit appropriate versions of journal articles to a repository; the challenge for researchers is to remember to perform this task after the primary work of the publication process is done. This case study at Brock University Library shows how it is possible to bootstrap these types of submissions by crafting meaningful publishing narratives through a collection of clever Open Access Week initiatives. title: How policy is reshaping open access: everything, everywhere, all at once - Research Consulting
content: "There’s a growing consensus from governments and funders around the world that publicly funded research should be published openly and preferably openly immediately. Where policymakers diverge is on the mechanism for achieving immediate open access (OA). That divergence is leading to a regionally fragmented publishing sector that creates a strategic problem for publishers: the funding routes they relied on are being withdrawn, and one global model no longer fits every market. In principle, none of this is new. Publishers have run differentiated regional strategies for years, but the pace and the stakes have changed. It also sits alongside other policy fronts moving just as fast, from how AI systems use and help produce scholarly content to questions of copyright and verification. Those issues deserve separate treatment; here, we’re focusing specifically on the rapidly changing policy and funding environment around open access."

title: Securing the digital future of open social sciences and humanities research - Research Information
content:
"New partnerships are formed, communities emerge, and innovative services are developed as a result. Yet forging collaboration is only the beginning. How do successful initiatives move beyond project formation and become sustainable parts of the research ecosystem?

The answer to that question lies within OPERAS’s journey towards becoming a European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC) a legal framework established by the European Commission to provide robust governance and a financially sustainable foundation for pan-European research collaboration.

OPERAS (Open scholarly Communication in the European Research Area for Social Sciences and Humanities) is a European collaboration created to strengthen open scholarly communication in the social sciences and humanities (SSH), bringing together publishers, libraries, researchers and infrastructure providers from across Europe. Through the newly launched OPERAS-PRIME project, the infrastructure is preparing for the next stage of its development, with the aim of achieving ERIC status by late 2027 or early 2028."

title: Who Needs National Journals? Dissemination Strategies in Canadian Scholarly Communication | The Canadian Journal of Information and Library Science
content: Abstract: The dominance of English-language journals marginalizes national and local scholarly publications. Focusing on Canada’s bilingual (English and French), community‑oriented and Open Access‑rich journal ecosystem, this study uses comprehensive data to ask who relies on Canadian journals, how language and research focus affect reach, and what that reveals about balancing local relevance with global visibility. Drawing on two major bibliometric databases (OpenAlex and Dimensions), we show that Canadian journals play a key role as venues for the dissemination of locally relevant research while also contributing to the global infrastructure for scholarly communication. Most articles published in Canadian journals are authored by researchers affiliated with foreign institutions, and most research authored by Canadians is published in journals based outside Canada. We find that Canadian authors are most likely to publish their work in national journals when they are in decision-making roles, when the language of publication is French, or when the topics are locally relevant. title: New UKRN reports highlight opportunities and limits of AI-powered monitoring of research data sharing | UK Reproducibility Network
content: "Two new reports from the UKRN – Working Paper 13: Monitoring Data Availability Statements and FAIR Data Practices in Medical Research Council (MRC)-Funded Research and UKRN Working Paper 14: Monitoring Data Sharing and FAIR Practices with LLMs – provide fresh evidence on how research funders and institutions can monitor data-sharing practices at scale, and what role artificial intelligence is likely to play in the future. Together, the reports address a growing challenge for research policy: how to assess whether publicly funded research data can be found, accessed and reused without relying on costly manual review of thousands of publications every year. While expectations around open research and FAIR data have become increasingly widespread, robust monitoring remains difficult. The first report examines a sample of 2023 publications acknowledging support from the Medical Research Council (MRC). It found that Data Availability Statements (DASs) were present in more than 80% of publications, but only around 59% were judged acceptable against established criteria. title: Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns | Nature
content:
"The co-founder of a prominent open-science platform has announced that funding uncertainties have forced the site to make changes to some of its most popular features.

In a statement released on 11 August, Brian Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science (COS) in Charlottesville, Virginia, which runs the Open Science Framework (OSF), announced that the platform will no longer allow researchers to post their code and data after 16 November. Any documents that are already publicly available on the site will remain online. But users will no longer be able to upload new materials in private mode.

The OSF’s preregistration workflow — which allows scientists to post research designs and articles that describe their planned methods and analyses for upcoming experiments — will continue to operate as normal, as will the 14 preprint servers run on the OSF platform."

title: Frontiers | Does Interdisciplinary Breadth Shape Research Data Sharing and Citation Impact? Evidence from Six Research Fields
content: Abstract: Research data sharing has become an important component of open science, yet sharing benefits vary across research contexts. Existing studies have examined factors influencing data sharing and the citation advantage associated with open data, but less is known about how interdisciplinary breadth relates to observable sharing practices and whether the citation advantage of sharing differs across disciplines. This study investigates the relationships among interdisciplinary breadth, observable sharing practices, and citation impact using 566,188 journal articles indexed in OpenAlex from 2020 to 2025. Interdisciplinary breadth was operationalized as the number of Level-0 disciplinary concepts associated with each article. Observable sharing practices were identified through repository links, supplementary-material links, and textual sharing statements. title: How to Build a Sovereign Global Knowledge Commons | Katina Magazine
content: "Scholarly publishing has its own potential single points of failure. The indexing databases, hosting platforms, and citation infrastructures of the Western scholarly record are concentrated among a small number of commercial owners, each exposed to the same risk. The point is not that a change of ownership at a scholarly publisher would make headlines like the Twitter takeover did. It is that the underlying structural condition—a single point of control over infrastructure that many depend on and few govern—is the same, and that the appropriate response is also the same: distribute governance and control rights before the acquisition or the political pressure occurs, not after."

title: Recommendations for Revising the Open Access Classification System in OpenAlex | Zenodo
content: "The open access (OA) color classification system used by Unpaywall (i.e., Gold, Green, Hybrid, Bronze, and closed) was introduced in 2018 and has since become widely used across the ecosystem, including by Scopus, Web of Science, Dimensions, and numerous funders and institutions worldwide. However, the scholarly communication landscape has changed significantly since these categories were defined and the limits of this system are proving problematic. In particular, the current system struggles with research outputs that are not journal publications, relies too heavily on journal-level policies rather than work-level attributes, conflates business models with access status, and is difficult to accurately operationalize in an environment where journals regularly change the OA status of publications en masse. The OpenAlex Colors Working Group was convened by the OpenAlex Community Advisory Board in January 2026 to evaluate these limitations and recommend a revised framework. title: Biomedical Publishing Metrics as a Barrier to Knowledge Dissemination
content: Abstract:  The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is an outdated biomedical metric that hinders knowledge dissemination. Relying on citation counts creates a skewed, easily manipulated system with a temporal lag that ignores global equity. Frontline clinicians consume research to improve care but rarely generate citations, meaning the JIF cannot capture real-world clinical utility. To ensure rankings reflect true value, publishers must adopt a multi-dimensional matrix prioritizing usage-based Altmetrics, such as verified downloads and views, to instantly measure global clinical application.

title: Unlocking knowledge: diamond open access publishing - UNESCO Digital Library
content: Diamond Open Access (OA) is an equitable scholarly publishing model that treats knowledge as a digital public good, with no fees for readers or authors. Built on shared infrastructure, open licensing, and community governance, it supports non-profit, academically driven publishing while allowing commercial providers to deliver specific services. Like Open Educational Resources (OER), Diamond OA promotes equitable access, collaboration, and multilingual knowledge sharing. It can strengthen national and institutional Open Access strategies while connecting OER, Open Data, and open research software into interoperable knowledge ecosystems. This brief examines Diamond OA infrastructure and provides practical policy guidance for Member States and institutions.

title: Up Close and Personal with the Trump Administration’s NIH Funding Cuts: An Interview with Sylvia Chou and Alexa Romberg - The Scholarly Kitchen
content: "More than 400,000 US federal employees have left their jobs during the second Trump administration – voluntarily or, in many cases, not. Even taking into account new hires since January 2025, there has been a net loss of 285,000 staff, many of whom had years, if not decades, of experience. Over 10,000 of them were experts in STEM and health fields, with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) especially hard hit, losing more than 1,100 staff – around 10% of its workforce. Among them were Sylvia Chou and Alexa Romberg, who chose to leave the organization as a result of the changes being made under NIH Director Dr Jay Bhattacharya. They were two of the original signatories of the Bethesda Declaration, an open letter to Dr Bhattacharya that expressed serious concerns about the changes being made under his leadership. Sylvia and Alexa are both involved in 27 UNIHTED (Sylvia as a Senior Advisor), an organization that was set up in 2025 as a way to continue supporting the integrity of publicly-funded health research in the United States.
